candidate.educational_objective: Use the label/SDS and the facility’s trained hazardous-chemical procedure to select appropriate controls and PPE before cleaning an unfamiliar chemical spill.

options.A: Continue routine work around the spill until symptoms develop because a small-appearing spill does not require hazard identification or protective measures.
options.B: Stop handling the chemical; consult the container label and Safety Data Sheet, then follow the facility’s trained spill or emergency procedure, including the specified exposure controls and PPE, before attempting cleanup.
options.C: Clean the spill immediately with bare hands and paper towels because rapid removal is safer than identifying the substance or obtaining appropriate protective equipment.
options.D: Evacuate the entire building for every chemical spill regardless of the substance, quantity, ventilation, exposure risk, or the facility’s hazardous-material procedure.

candidate.rationale: OSHA’s Hazard Communication Standard requires hazardous-chemical labels, Safety Data Sheets, and worker training that includes measures for protection such as emergency procedures, work practices, engineering controls, and PPE. When the chemical is unfamiliar, the safe response is to identify the hazard through the label/SDS and follow the employer’s trained procedure before cleanup rather than improvising.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Workers must have chemical hazard information through labels/SDSs and training on the employer’s protective/emergency procedures, controls, and PPE.
